extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and modes of treatment (dramatic vs pictorial) in novels: how to place narrators, when to dramatize or survey, how to use scenes, and how to balance authorial and character voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / relation of narrator to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole question of method in the craft of fiction is governed by the question of the point of view — the relation in which the narrator stands to the story: he tells it as he sees it, and the reader faces the story-teller and listens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the narrator is presented as an external storyteller, a character in the story, or omitted; the narrator’s position determines what can be shown or asserted. If the storyteller's presence becomes distracting, consider introducing alternative points of view or dramatizing to shift responsibility from the author to a spokesman within the book. Evaluate how the narrator’s stance affects authority, arbitrariness, and the reader’s trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization / showing (enactment while it happens)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic story never deviates from a strictly scenic form: one episode follows another with no interruption for reflective summary; nobody expounds or explains — the story is enacted by its look and behaviour at particular moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatization when the subject benefits from immediate, visible action. Advantages: objectivity, vividness, and the highest degree of authority. Limitations: drama is confined to what eye and ear can perceive and generally excludes direct access to private thoughts. Choose dramatization when you want scenes to present things directly rather than describe them retrospectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an in-story spokesman narrator (bringing authorial voice into the book)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the storyteller is in the story himself the author is dramatized; his assertions gain weight because they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing a spokesman/narrator within the story disguises arbitrary authorial assertion by making claims accountable to a visible character. This can make the narrative self-contained and reduce the sense of external authorial intrusion. Consider this to increase plausibility of assertions without losing control of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial / panoramic method (retrospective narration and survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pictorial book the narrator (author or a creature of the book) gathers up experience and composes a vision of it; it is a reflection of experience that allows general, panoramic survey, wanderings in time and space, and accumulation of impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial method where the story is too comprehensive or widely ranging for strict scenic form — for long periods, panoramas, and accumulated impressions. The narrator’s voice is central here; expect retrospection, summation, and commentary. Beware of thinness; the narrator’s mind becomes the object and can itself be dramatized to avoid flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique narration / third-person limited (author supplements character’s vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: By changing first person to third, the author may use the man's field of vision while remaining free in time; the narrator’s picture is the character’s yet reinforced by the author's mind — there are effectively two brains behind the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oblique (third-person-limited) narration to retain a fixed spatial viewpoint while gaining temporal flexibility and the author's supplementing intelligence. This reduces the insistence of a single narrator’s voice, enriches the picture, and allows the author to add touches beyond the character’s immediate sensation without violating point-of-view consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration: fixed position and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator speaks in the first person there can be no uncertainty in point of view; his account represents the face that the facts in sequence turned towards him, and he cannot leave his fixed position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person provides a distinct, bounded perspective with clarity about limits of knowledge and vision. It restricts access to other minds and disallows temporal liberties the author might want; it’s powerful for intimate, self-contained perspectives but unsuitable when the subject requires broader or shifting views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject dictates method (choose dramatization or picture according to theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: How far dramatization should be pushed depends entirely upon the kind of effect the theme demands: the subject dictates the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before selecting forms, determine where the burden of the story lies (e.g., a study of a soul versus a panoramic social history). Don’t force a subject into an inappropriate form: introspective or character-growth themes often require non-dramatic, pictorial treatment; whereas action-oriented material may thrive under dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: The scene’s primacy and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident, the scene, properly so called, comes first in importance beyond doubt; a novelist instinctively sees chief turns and phases of his story expressed as things acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the placement and construction of scenes as a prime concern. Scenes deliver the sharpest effects and should be used where emphasis must fall most strongly. Plan where scenes will mark structural turning points and climaxes rather than scattering dramatic presentation indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene economy and limitations (scenes are time-space expensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a scene, as it appears to the reader, it displays the whole of the time and space it occupies; it cannot cover more of either than it actually renders and is therefore expensive in time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes sparingly and strategically because they consume narrative length. For conveying long stretches, use oblique narration or summary to economize. Reserve full dramatic scenes for moments that need immediate, visible demonstration (clinching events, climaxes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare scenes in advance (don’t let scenes bear tasks they’re unprepared for)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene which is not in some way prepared in advance is a scene which in point of fact is wasting a portion of its strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up antecedent narrative, tension, or context so that a scene can deliver a concentrated effect. Prepared scenes act swiftly and sharply; unprepared scenes may feel thin or overburdened and diminish impact. Use previous picture or narrative to build toward the scene’s payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid squandering scenes / unnecessary dramatic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelists are often over-shy of availing themselves of the fully wrought scene, and conversely they often break into dialogue and dramatic presentation when there is nothing to be gained by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t default to immediate dramatization simply because it’s lively; evaluate whether the scene adds structural or emotional value. If it doesn't clinch or advance a matter significantly, prefer oblique narrative, summary, or pictorial treatment to preserve dramatic force for pivotal moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermittent objectivity for central consciousness (closing the seer’s mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author can, without awkwardness, allow his central seer’s act of vision to lapse and make the hero impenetrable at times so that he drops into the plane of the other characters and can be treated like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story is centered in a single consciousness, periodically withdrawing direct access to that consciousness (making it opaque) lets the character be seen objectively through dialogue and action. This prevents the central character from dissolving into a vague blur and gives him more dramatic presence among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial weakness into strength by dramatizing the narrator’s mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When you recall and picture an impression in words you give a sight of things in a mirror; you can dramatize the mirror (the narrator’s mind) and make it a visible object, converting a disability into a new kind of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the pictorial/retrospective mode risks thinness, deliberately emphasize and dramatize the narrator’s consciousness—the ‘mirror’—so that the reader sees the mind that mediates the picture. This yields a distinctive effect and avoids flat reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial (minstrel’s) licence is the easiest but narrow method
rubrics_metrics.description: The old unguarded way where the author alone entertains the reader — his voice confessedly and alone — imposes no limitation and is the easiest way; but it is often a narrower method that curtails the story’s possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve an overt, authorial voice for writers who can sustain the effect without losing advantages of more varied methods. Generally, prefer methods that make fuller use of dramatization and pictorial balances; relying only on the author’s voice can restrict drama and subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a working theory of technical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: In the handling of his book a novelist must have some working theory to guide him — some theory of the relative uses and values of the different means at his disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a conscious sense of when to use scenes, panoramas, narrator voices, oblique narration, and first-person constraints. Study exemplars and form a hierarchy of techniques for different narrative needs rather than relying purely on inclination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance drama and picture (picture lays groundwork; drama delivers final stroke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture, the general survey with command of time and space, finds its opportunity where a long reach is more needed than sharp visibility; drama gives the final stroke which it is adapted to deliver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use picture to accumulate impressions, set context, and handle expanses of time or space; use drama to deliver culmination, demonstration, and decisive moments. Build picture and drama to support each other rather than substituting one for the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panorama/picture to accumulate impressions over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture travels over periods and expanses, pausing here, driving off into the distance there, making no account of bounds of a particular occasion; its office is to pile up an accumulated impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pictorial methods when you need to present social context, cultural panoramas, or long-term developments that cannot be dramatized economically. Combine pictorial accumulation with later scenes that crystallize and validate the impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic form excludes private mind access in rigid drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In rigid drama there is naturally no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters; their thoughts and motives are transmuted into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your design requires strict scenic objectivity (as in plays), plan how motives and inner life will be externalized through dialogue and behaviour. For interiority-driven subjects, avoid rigid drama that would strangle the theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of author and character voices reduces narrator insistence (benefit of oblique narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In oblique narration the sound of the narrator’s voice is less insistent because another voice is speedily mixed and blended with it; the picture contains the character’s vision reinforced by the author’s wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a blended voice to achieve richness without authoritarian intrusion: allow the character’s perspective to dominate while letting the author subtly supplement. This achieves both vividness and wider informational/temporal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes should clinch matters rather than perform all work
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene should be used supremely to clinch a matter already pending, to demonstrate a result, to crown an effect half-made by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure narrative so that scenes are moments of confirmation or decisive revelation — not the primary means to create all necessary context. Let picture, summary, and earlier incidents build toward scenes that then deliver the final, concentrated effect.
